utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So good morning, Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-68, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Oric, can you follow the proceedings in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. I can follow everything in my own mother tongue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I am not receiving interpretation, but there is a simple explanation to it: I am on number 0. Okay. I thank you, Mr. Oric, and good morning to you. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, and also good morning to my learned friends of the Defence. My name is Jan Wubben, lead counsel for the Prosecution. I am here together with co-counsel, Mr. Gramsci Di Fazio, Ms. Joanne Richardson, and our case manager, Mrs. Donnica Henry-Frijlink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you and good morning to you and your team, of course, Mr. Wubben. Appearances for Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I'm Vasvija Vidovic. Together with Mr. John Jones I represent Mr. Oric. We have our legal assistant, Ms. Jasmina Cosic, and our case manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you and good morning to you as well and to the rest of your team. So any preliminaries before we bring in the witness? I just wanted to alert you to the fact that although two days ago I said and you agreed with me at the time that there was probably no need for a written decision on the protective measures that we discussed at the end of the day. We decided that it is more in conformity of the practice we have been following so far and we handed down a written decision. So you should have received that; I signed it yesterday. Yes, the other thing you had to come back to me, you remember I mentioned to you, saying that it was something that we will deal with first thing on Wednesday morning regarding the CD containing the photos of the site visit. And that I agreed -- or we agreed that it should not be a party exhibit but a Court exhibit. So do you have anything to add in relation to this matter? Mr. Wubben?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, regarding that CD, first issue: We consent to accepting the index provided to us this morning as being an accurate reflection of the photos as much as possible. Of course, when it comes to photographs taken from the helicopter, and that's confirmed, I noticed it. That's the first issue. There's a second issue: We want to tender a translation, an English translation, of the book of -- with the title "Srebrenica" by Ibisevic. We already used that book prior to the summer break during the second witness, and that was a part of it. But now we can hand over a total English translation of that book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you, Mr. Wubben. Is there -- are there any remarks from the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours. We have nothing to add in relation to photos and the index. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And -- yeah, and in relation to the translation on the book that the Prosecution is seeking to tender?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we would like to thank the Prosecution since we will be using the said book a great deal in the course of the proceedings. At any rate, Your Honours, we will look through the translation, and if we happen to have any comments we shall react accordingly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, obviously. I thank you, Madam Vidovic. So let's close this chapter first -- one moment --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, apologies. In addition, for your information, it was accepted that part of the translation was accepted under P564 during that second witness's cross-examination, for your information, to assign a new P number to that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm going to give it a number. So let's get the help of Madam Registrar. Let's start with this translation of Ibisevic's book. You've heard Mr. Wubben say that it was P564. Shall we give it P564.1 or what do you -- what is your preference in order not to create confusion for you?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, it will be P564E, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: E. So this will be P564E. All right. And the CD-ROM with the photos of the site visit, this will be a Court document so it will be C or a CT? I don't know?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be C2.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And the typewritten index will be C2.1?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Good. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I am also being reminded that some time back I had also suggested that we will also have the CD containing the reconnaissance pictures taken by Mr. Berikoff to be included also amongst the exhibits. If there's no objection to that that will be so admitted and marked as Exhibit C3. Okay. All right. So this will be Exhibit C3. Any further preliminaries?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Madam Hotic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before I proceed any further, I want to make sure that what I am saying in English and what will be said in English later on is being translated to you in a language that you can understand. Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If at any time there are problems with the reception of interpretation, either you're not receiving it or it's too loud or you cannot hear it well enough, please draw our attention straight away and we will rectify the matter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So good morning and welcome to this Tribunal. You have been summoned to give evidence in this trial against Naser Oric. You've been summoned as a Defence witness. And very soon you will sit down and start giving evidence, but before you do so our rules require that you enter a solemn declaration equivalent to an oath in several jurisdictions, domestic jurisdictions, namely that in the course your testimony you will be testifying the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text is contained in a piece of paper which the lady usher standing next to you is going to hand you now. Please read it out aloud and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam, you may sit down and make yourself comfortable. And I'll explain to you very briefly what's going to happen. As I said, you have been summoned by the Defence as one of their witnesses, so it will be the Defence, Mr. Jones precisely, who will be asking you questions. He will then be followed by Mr. Di Fazio, who is appearing -- one of the counsels appearing for the Prosecution in this case. Your responsibility and your obligation under the solemn declaration that you have just made is to answer all questions irrespective of where they are coming from, irrespective of who is putting the questions to you, to answer all these questions fully and honestly and to the best of your ability. Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Could you please give the Court your full name.

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: My name is Kada Hotic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And if you could confirm for us the following personal details: You were born on the 11th of May, 1945, in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your father went missing during the Second World War and your mother remarried?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And growing up you had two brothers, Ekrem Cilovic and Mustafa Cilovic as well as a sister, Rukja?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You were married to Sead Hotic in 1965?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You had a son called Samir and a daughter Lejla.

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And your husband, your son, and your two brothers were all killed when Srebrenica fell to the Serbs in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you lose many other relatives in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: All my male relatives. Some families -- some family names disappeared altogether. There are no male relatives left bearing that -- those family names.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Are you involved in any association which is dedicated to preserving the memory of those who died in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm an active member and a deputy president of the movement of the mothers of the enclaves of Srebrenica and Zepa. Those were the enclaves which were under the protection of the UN, and they went through what they went through in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, from 1973 until the fall of Srebrenica, did you live in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And where did you live?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: The Marsal Tito Street next to the post office and the hospital. Those two buildings still stand in Srebrenica today.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And where did your two brothers live?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: The Stari Grad Street in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did they know Akif Ustic?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. We were close.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, before the war your husband worked in the JNA and then left to study sociology part time, eventually becoming a professor of sociology. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Can you tell us briefly why he left the JNA?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: In 1970 my husband left the JNA service because he felt that there was discrimination against him. He had the wish to go on to higher education, but he was always told that he was good enough for the job he had, whereas his colleagues who were Serbs were sent off to higher education institutions. He was revolted and he left the job, and there were other reasons as well. He could feel that discrimination as early as the 1970s.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And this was discrimination against him as a Bosniak?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course, because he was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: His last job before retiring was at the Ministry of the Interior in Srebrenica. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Perhaps you misunderstood me. The Ministry of the Interior -- yeah, that's where he worked, at SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. It might have been a problem with translation. I was referring to the Ministry of the Interior, the SUP. When did he leave the SUP?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was the SUP. He retired in 1991, in the beginning of 1991. I can't recall the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. Now, it's not in dispute that war broke out in Bosnia in 1992. Were you aware of any events locally prior to war breaking out which were in any way out of the ordinary?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Some things started to happen which appeared a bit weird. Where I worked, and it was a clothes factory, there were 250 women working there, Serbs, Muslims, Croats, and then rumours started about the Serbs being threatened, about how something had to be done. And occasionally we complained about this. We asked why they felt that the Serbs were threatened. And then there was a problem in Slovenia when the JNA soldiers were attacked. And then we felt sorry for the soldiers, all of us together, because we felt that they were our soldiers, the soldiers of the former Yugoslavia. And then war broke out in Vukovar, and the same army, the JNA, attacked the population of Vukovar and crimes were perpetrated there. And we still believed that war would not come to Bosnia. We still worked together. But during our breaks our Serb colleagues tended to sit apart and they had their own story going. They said that the Serb brethren should be helped. And one of my colleagues was called Rosa said, Oh, I've got a pig that I'm going to send to Knin, there are Serbs living there and they are threatened and they should be helped. And we never quite understood why they needed any assistance and why they felt they were threatened in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. In your factory was there talk about Radovan Karadzic or Slobodan Milosevic? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Those were the top political leaders and they addressed the public through the media. And we always commented on their statements in the course of our breaks. And those of us who were Muslims or Bosniaks never agreed with them because we really did not know why they were spreading that propaganda, according to which the Serbs were threatened, that they should all live in one state. And when Karadzic said that if the Muslims ever resisted they would be wiped off the face of the earth, I mean it was unclear to us why the Muslim people should be made to disappear and why we should be considered obstacles to one other in Bosnia at the time. Slobodan Milosevic was the top political leader in Serbia, and our Serb colleagues applauded his speeches and they adored him. And also there was the radical Serb leader Seselj, and when he got there my Serb colleagues said, Thank God that man has come along who is likely to lead our youth on the right path. But it was still unclear to us what was brewing. We felt that it was going to blow over, that those political changes and speeches and everything would stop. But we were betrayed, in fact, because not a single colleague or friend or boss of some kind or a leader within the municipality of Srebrenica never gave us any hint of what was in the making. They kept everything secret.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Hotic. I just want to stop you there to ask you this: Did your husband ever speak to you about events which he noticed occurring locally which caused him alarm?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Even before the beginning of the war, my husband noticed some things that were not quite clear to him. For example, while he was still working he went out into the field, he went to Skelani, this is on the Drina river in the municipality of Srebrenica, and he noticed a group of people having target practice. They were using ammunition, rifles. And in view of the fact that Savo Aleksic, his chief of SUP was there, he asked Savo, Savo, do you know why they are shooting over there, why are they having target practice, because any firing from a firearm, for that you had to have permission from the SUP. Savo said he had no idea what was going on there. Also, trees were being cut, roads were being cut through the hills around Srebrenica so that my husband also was asking, Why are these trees being cut? Why are these roads being cut through? And they said it was for the export of timber three years before the war broke out. However, the Territorial Defence weapons from the municipality of Srebrenica were withdrawn to the zone headquarters without any explanation why this was being done. Of course, my husband, because he was amongst the prominent people in Srebrenica, was asking why this was happening but he never received an explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: There's three events you mention, and I'll just try to fix each of them in time. The shooting in the Skelani area, when did that occur, roughly?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: The shooting was in 1991 at the beginning of the year, I think, but please don't ask me for the exact date because I really don't remember the date. I remember the events, but I've forgotten the dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. And the woods -- sorry, the roads which were being built through the woods, again when did that occur roughly?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: That was also in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And then finally, the surrender of the weapons of the TO to the district staff which you described, when did that occur?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: That was three years before the war broke out.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And in each case your husband asked his superior, Savo Aleksic, what was going on and he received the answer that Savo didn't know. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Not only Savo Aleksic, he asked him when he was his superior but he was also asking the top men in the Srebrenica municipality. Mostly it was the Serbs who were at these positions. For example, the chief of the Territorial Defence was Miso Stanisaljevic and he asked him about the weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And Miso Stanisaljevic and Savo Aleksic are both Serbs. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did your husband draw any conclusions about these activities which he observed?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: It was just suspicious. He didn't really know exactly what was going on, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In terms of those new roads which you mentioned, subsequently were they used for anything during the course of the war?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: All those roads and the places where the forest was cut through so you could have a view of Srebrenica, the Serbs placed tanks and mortars and other artillery weapons so that they could shoot at Srebrenica. And that is where they fired at Srebrenica, from these positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. Now, I'm going to move on to the war now in early 1992. Was anything done by people in Srebrenica, in Bratunac municipalities to prevent conflict from breaking out in those municipalities?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Before the conflict broke out, the most prominent men in Srebrenica spoke with the Serbs, first of all with the president of the SDS, Goran Zekic, and with other people in order to reach some kind of agreement to prevent a conflict, to see what they could do in order to continue living together, since we had lived and worked together before. But there were several meetings that took place in Srebrenica, in Bratunac, in the Fontana Hotel, in Ljubovic, at Brioni, and I remember Dr. Sabit Begic, he was a doctor. These were not military people. These were just intellectuals from different professions. Sabit was a doctor, for example, an internist, Gasi Fustic [as interpreted] was a professor at school.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'll stop you there for a moment. It's come out as Gasi Fustic. Is that the correct name? Or could you repeat the name of the person who was a professor at school.

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Kijasev Ostic [as interpreted] and many people were aware that something was going on and that something had to be done. Of course, they had meetings with Zekic and other Serbs. They spoke with them several times. Even Kijasev was offering his children as a kind of guarantee in exchange for his own children. They would put each other's children in each other's apartment as some kind of safety guarantee. But after a number of meetings, suddenly Dr. Sabit Begic passed by the -- along the street and I heard him say, There will be a war, you better save yourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. I think I still need to clarify this name. I'll approach it this way. Earlier I asked you if your two brothers lived near -- or you told us that your two brothers lived near Akif Ustic. The person that you're referring to as being involved in these discussions, is that Akif Ustic or is it some other --

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: I apologise, Akif, yes, not Kijasev. Please, forgive me. Akif. I apologise, it's my mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And so Akif Ustic, he proposed to Goran Zekic, is that correct, that his children would stay --

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: -- as a sort of guarantee of peace. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did Goran Zekic accept that offer?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Why was Akif Ustic involved in these discussions?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: People were simply looking for some kind of solution. The situation was difficult, and of course in order to prevent a war, because Muslims, Bosniaks in Srebrenica did not want a war. They didn't have the means and they have any need for war. We thought that we could live the same way that we lived before. I don't know why we would need to have a war in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Then you told us that Dr. Sabit Begic after a certain number of these meetings said that there will be war, that you better save yourselves. What was the reaction to that announcement?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: There were many people at that time who had a car and who heard that and they left Srebrenica that day. And most of those people are still alive today, including Sabit Begic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And among the people who left Srebrenica, was it all classes of people or was it a particular class or people with a certain level of education?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: It was mostly Muslims. Muslims. There were different profiles. There were educated people, those who understood that they could be in danger and that they should leave in order to save themselves. However, barricades were set up quite soon after that. I was also trying to persuade my husband and my son to leave. My husband said, though, that, I'm not guilty of anything. I don't want to be going all over the place. I think the situation would calm down and we should stay here.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So when did the barricades go up and it become impossible to leave Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: The barricades were set up in April 1992 so we couldn't leave anymore. It was in late March and early April; nobody could leave Srebrenica anymore after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And at a certain stage did the Serbs take over the SUP and fire the Muslims from there?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: In the meantime the Serbs evacuated their families, their wives, and children from Srebrenica, and we were wondering why they were doing that. The people who stayed were men who dressed in former JNA uniforms. My neighbours, Serbs, all dressed in former JNA uniforms. They simply disbanded the police, the milicija, at the time, the Muslims that were there. The chief at the time, Hamed Efendic, was dismissed as well. And they took over all the key structures in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, did there come a time when you had to leave your house in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. We simply sensed danger because my neighbours, Serbs, had taken up arms, and those who had left Srebrenica had left, and those who had stayed behind, stayed behind. We were simply trying to save ourselves by staying close to the woods. My brothers had a house that was closest to the woods, so we went to their place and we were simply waiting for something to be resolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Was there ever any specific event which led to you actually spending the night or nights in the woods?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: We were still staying at my brother's place. It snowed even though it was not -- it was still -- it was not the usual time for it to snow. The fruit trees for already blossoming. So we could hear some shelling in the area of Potocari, and my husband said that he assumed that these were mortars because he was an expert in weapons, he knew about weapons. That morning, a neighbour came. We called him our neighbour, he was Drago Andric from Pribicevac. It's a village two kilometres away from Srebrenica, you go through Stari Grad. So he came to my brother's place in order to use the telephone because they didn't have a telephone up there. He had sons in Novi Sad, so we wanted to talk to him. So we asked him, Drago, what is happening? He said, We are attacking the Green Berets. And we said, What Green Berets, Drago? And he said, There are Green Berets. So we said, Well, what are we going to do, Drago? And he said, Well, come back up to my place. And then my brother, my son, my husband and I all went to Pribicevac, to Drago's place, and we spent the night there. During the night a Niva vehicle passed by the road that had been cut through the hills. It was a red Niva car and Drago went out and then he came back laughing. And we said, Drago, what is happening? And he said, Well, they've just brought a mortar over. So I said, What are we going to do with a mortar? And he said, Well, we will set it up at Tri Kralja, that's what the place was called, and that's where we will shell Srebrenica from. And I said, Why would you want to do that? He said, Well, because of the Green Berets. In the course of the night he went out two or three times and then he said the Tri Kralja location is not suitable. Another location, Divlivac [phoen], it's much better to be able to shell Srebrenica. So we spent the night there. And then I told my husband and my brother, let's go home because somebody from the army could come because they were expecting somebody. His wife is making bread and it's only her and her husband who are at home. So I thought maybe some soldiers would come by, and I didn't want anybody to abuse us, mistreat us or maybe mistreat those people because of us. So in the morning I said, Drago, could you please take us through the forest and after that bring us to some place where we could find our own way because I think it would be the best thing to return to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. So that's -- could you fix the date, first of all, when this event occurred?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: I can't tell you the exact date. It was in late April, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Late April 1992, I take it?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Drago, can you tell us his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Drago was a Serb, and the village of Pribicevac had three or four Serb houses. His brother Srecko was there. Also a family called Vukosavljevic. There was also another young man.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do I take it from this -- from what you saw that you saw a mortar being placed in Pribicevac in 1992, being brought to Pribicevac?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: I heard that from Drago. A car passed and Drago said that there was a mortar in it. I didn't go out to look.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And subsequently were you aware whether or not artillery was placed on Pribicevac?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. When we came home that morning, I don't know whether it was on that same day or the next day, we wanted to return to our apartment in Srebrenica. But we came to Lovac and that's where we heard shooting. In front of the Domavija hotel and we returned because of this shooting. We didn't know who was shooting or why. Very soon after that we could hear shouting over a loud speaker through the Petrica and Crni Guber Streets. We were at an elevated point between those two streets, and we could hear clearly that they were asking people who possessed legal or illegal weapons to surrender them, otherwise those people found to be in possession of weapons would be slaughtered. We were in a panic, and all the people in Stari Grad, we all went Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. to one house in a panic and then we simply all agreed that we would go to the woods. So we fled to the woods although --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry if I cut you off occasionally but you're giving very detailed answers, and actually it would be helpful if you give slightly less detail on -- at least it's not necessary to give as much detail for each of these questions.

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The question which I -- which I'd appreciate you answering is whether -- in Pribicevac whether you became aware during the course of 1992 of heavy artillery or any sort of artillery being placed there?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. While we were in the woods. One afternoon, the firing started. They started to shell with mortars, and that day I counted 83 mortars fired. And I could hear clearly the instruction from the command: Fire at Karsija. This is a forest. And Akif Ustic, Hakija Meholjic went to that forest as well as a group of young met to think about what they would do, how to set up a defence because we were attacked, and we had to figure out how to defend ourselves. My son still hadn't joined them, he was still with us, but very soon after that he also went there to join them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. But please just try to answer the question I pose, because I want to stick specifically with Pribicevac for a moment. You mentioned -- you've confirmed that there was artillery in Pribicevac. Did that change during the course of 1992 or was there always Serb artillery in Pribicevac?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: From that place you could see -- actually, that place from the Srebrenica marketplace, the square, you could see where that forest was cut through. That was the place where they fired mortars at the town. Later they also fired tank grenades. There were also PAM and PAT weapons, and these were very large weapons with a range good enough to be able to hit the centre of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You say that was the place where they fired mortars, you're referring to Pribicevac?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And if someone were to say that in, let's say, the summer of 1992 it was perfectly possible for Muslims to pass through Pribicevac to go from Srebrenica to, let's say, Mocevici or Poznanovici, would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: It was impossible because you had to pass through their ambushes and how could you do that, the Serb ambushes or the Serb positions were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, you've mentioned that when you came back from going to Pribicevac the first time with Drago that then someone was going around with a speaker telling Muslims, I think it was, to disarm. So I want to ask you a question or two about that. First of all, who was doing that? Who was going around with a megaphone?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: When I mentioned the shooting, because of which we returned and tried to go back to our apartment because we still thought it was possible to stay there, that's when the White Eagles came. Later we found out that the White Eagles went to Srebrenica or entered Srebrenica. After their stay, I don't know how long they stayed, they ransacked all the apartments, houses, looking for weapons. Many women brought out hunting rifles, or if somebody had a pistol or something, because they were afraid that the men would leave. The men were in the forest. So they collected everything and they also took away the cars. And one of my neighbours who asked a young man when she took the hunting rifle to him, she asked him, You are so young and so handsome, please be careful, child, not to get killed somewhere. Don't make your mother cry. And he said, I am paid to do this, and then I will leave. I am not even from here, I am from Nis. Nis is in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So this young man from Nis in Serbia was a White Eagle?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. She said he had a nice jacket, a nice clean sneakers, he had a neat haircut, he looked very neat. He wasn't wearing a uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And were -- was it only White Eagles who were involved in disarming Muslims in Srebrenica in this period or were local Serbs also involved?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Of course the local Serbs, too. There was a person, I can't remember his name, we called him Zmiro, Miodrag. He had occupied the SUP at the time and he had men who were asking for rifles. Some of the Muslims bought a rifle for 1500 German marks, and they wanted those rifles to be returned. They would give the number of the rifle, when it was sold, and for how much it was sold, so then they had to return those weapons. They went together to collect the weapons if -- however many pieces of firearms there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So you're saying that there was a way of knowing which Muslims had weapons because it was registered in some way. Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. Probably in the beginning people didn't know that all of this was being recorded when they bought the rifles. Later this became clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. Now, going back to the woods, how long did you spend in the woods?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: We spent 11 nights in the forest. After the snow, then it began to rain.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you know what happened to Muslims who remained in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: At one point, Eso Jakupovic came; he was a policeman. He came and told us not to go home at any cost because whatever people were found in Srebrenica were taken in front of the SUP and shot. There were 29 people. Amongst them was a former employee of the SUP. He was walking on crutches, he was an invalid, and they sent him to negotiate about something with Akif Ustic. I don't know what they were talking about. They kept his wife as a hostage, and this man, Eso, had to go back. But a total of 29 people were killed. All the people who remained in Srebrenica and didn't manage go to the woods were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you've mentioned a couple of times that Akif Ustic and I think you said Hakija Meholjic were in the woods as well. How many people in your group in total in that part of the woods?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Akif Ustic and Hakija Meholjic had a group of people from Petrica and Stari Grad. These were places that were close by. However, women, children, and my husband and my brother were on the other side of the woods, so I don't know exactly how many people were in the woods.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So the people you were with were those from Stari Grad and Petrica?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And were these all men in the woods or were there other women like you, were there children there?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: No, women and children. There were some elderly men. There were also some young men. Later the young men went to join Hakija and Akif.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: At that time did you have any weapons or anything like that with you?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: No, we didn't have any weapons, the women and the children. Maybe Hakija had some rifles. These were part of the police reserve forces, so they did have something. I know that my son told me that they had a few bullets each in their pockets, but that was all.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And what did you do for shelter at night?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: No, well, we didn't have any kind of shelter. We had a piece of tent fabric which we stretched out over the branches in order to cover ourselves or protect ourselves from the rain. We also covered ourselves with leaves and so on in order to stay warm. At night we would sneak back to our homes to bake bread so that we would have something to eat, something to feed our children with. We spent a total of 11 nights in the woods. I think I can give you the date for that. This was the 7th or the 8th of May when there was talk that Goran Zekic was killed. We felt relieved in a way, as if we were saved in a way. So then we spent a few more nights in the forest after that, and then we returned home.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And while you were in the woods, did you see any movement by the Serbs in Srebrenica? Did you see what they were doing?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: My brother had binoculars and we could see from the hill down into what was going on in Srebrenica. In Srebrenica there were trucks driving off furniture through Bojna. This was something that we could see, and then you could drive further towards Skelani Bajina Basta and so on. Anyway, they were carting of everything valuable from Srebrenica. Before that the White Eagles had taken away all the cars, so Srebrenica was abandoned. Perhaps a day or two after these things were being carted off, Srebrenica was torched from the entrance to the town all along the two streets. Srebrenica is a town with two streets. The houses that were very close to the woods were not fired -- torched. Everything else was set on fire. And then the Serbs left Srebrenica, and then two or three days after that we slowly started to return to Srebrenica because everything was being robbed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just one remark, my brother said -- she said that my brother is a gajodeta [phoen], a surveyor by profession, and that is something that did not get into the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I just want -- I wouldn't have any doubt that she did say so, I just want a confirmation from the witness. Did you say that your brother was a surveyor by profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, he was a surveyor by profession.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. One moment, Mr. Jones. Judge Eser.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: I would have a question just to clarify the area where it was this happened. When you speak of the woods or the forest, was it in the direction to Pribicevac or was it on the other side of Srebrenica? You talked about Pribicevac, where you had Serb mortars located. Now, could you perhaps describe where you, the Muslims, stayed during the night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Srebrenica hills are rather interesting, those are elevations and then creeks. The Pribicevac area was behind us. We were at the foot of the hill called Pribicevac. Shells flew over our heads, and they went in the direction of Karsija, which is the second hill. And all that is pretty close. I can't tell you in any other way.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Perhaps it's useful at this stage to hand up copies of a map which we've put together for this witness. In proofing this witness, I don't think she's particularly keen on locating places on a map. It's more really for our benefit. And just for the record this map, in order to Fakovici on the same map as Srebrenica, we did have to put together two maps, but they are perfectly aligned, I would submit, and one is a topographical map of Zvornik, the scale is 1:100.000, and the other one is a topographical map of Valjevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is, it seems to me at least, to be identical to D714. It's taken from the same survey map.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. I may use D714 later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not even a survey map.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And if it's -- yes, it's been placed on the ELMO, but I think we see Bojna south of Srebrenica and Pribicevac to the south-east.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Should we give it a number straight away, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. That would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This will be Defence Exhibit D --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I think it might be 716.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, it will be B715 --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: D715. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Hotic, you were telling us how you went back into Srebrenica. Can you just tell us briefly in what state you found the town when you returned?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: There wasn't a soul in town. There was nobody there. When we entered the town and we walked down the streets we saw burnt down houses, some totally burnt down, some only partially. In some cases half a house was left standing or a couple of rooms were left standing. But all houses had been broken in, all furniture was in disarray, whatever was of value was taken away, and it was a ghost town. And then we all went to our own places and we tried to make at least a little bit of those homes habitable. Only the apartment buildings next to the hospital were not set on fire, but all the houses as of the bus station and higher up, and that part on the way out from Srebrenica was not set on fire, so it was possible for us to spend some time there. But everything had been looted.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did you ever speak to anyone in Srebrenica who had actually been an eye-witness to the burning of houses?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I talked to Hasa Selmanagic. She was at the very centre of town near the mosque. She had a house there, and she didn't manage to flee to the woods, and she tried to defend her house and she was trying to put the fire out. There were only two or three people setting fire to houses because we could actually see them using the binoculars. And I even know the guy, he was called Tanto, and he was carrying a pail and he was throwing something into the houses. And Tanto is still in Srebrenica, and this woman almost went mad out of fear and horror. Because when her house was set on fire and another building was set on fire across the street next to the mosque, it was called the forestry building, there were people who were disabled who had stayed in, and they were set on fire alive, and they were burnt alive and they were screaming horribly. And later on we found out that eight people were actually burnt to death and their remains were buried near the mosque in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, Tanto you say is still in Srebrenica. Was he a local Serb?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. And he was called Tanto, it was his nickname, but I never knew what his real name was, and he lived in Carsija.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And from what you could see of the local Serbs in Srebrenica with the binoculars when you were in the woods, were they in civilian clothes Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. or in uniforms?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. The Serbs were wearing the uniforms of the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And were the Serbs -- when you refer to local Serbs, is that Serbs only from the town of Srebrenica, or did you at any stage notice or hear of Serbs from surrounding villages who were involved in the torching and looting of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. From the surrounding villages, from Orahovica I used to see them. They were together with our local Serbs from Srebrenica, neighbours. And basically they were all our neighbours because it is all in the same municipality. Except for when Arkan's or Seselj's men came along, or the White Eagles, they used to come and go as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. Now, it is not in dispute that Srebrenica was under intensive shelling at the time relevant to the indictment, so I'm not going to ask you about that in detail. I would ask you if you could locate for us where, to your knowledge, some of the locations the Serbs were shelling the town of Srebrenica in 1992.

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: From the direction of Pribicevac, Sase, Bratunac, and then opposite -- across Suceska, from Koprivno, from Rogac, from Tara, from all four sides basically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, this line of questioning is of course not one that I object to, but I would object to the witness providing this sort of evidence unless there's a foundation for it, the basis upon which she can say to you with accuracy and with reliability the point at which the shells emanated from. That's a complex business as far as I can understand, and unless this witness is qualified and can speak with some authority about that, the answer shouldn't be given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would have imagined, and in fact I was thinking exactly about the same matter, and I was waiting to see whether Mr. Jones actually would follow up with questions as to what basis she can be so categoric.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I'm sure you will do that, Mr. Jones. If you don't, obviously then -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And I certainly will. And maybe at the same time the types of weapons which were firing and how she knows which weapons were fired from where.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. I thank you, Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So we'll go through one by one. How do you know or why do you say that there was shelling from Pribicevac?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: From Pribicevac when they started shelling for the first time I heard the orders. They said, Go on like that, shoot in the direction of the main street, that's where the Green Berets are. Because it was close enough and we were at the foot of the hill from where they were shelling. So those were the first mortar shells. And my husband told me that they were -- I can't remember what exactly the calibre it was. But afterwards the other shells that were coming in from that area, it was coming from the direction of Sase or Koprivno Brdo. Afterwards we found out that the name of the hill was Koprivno Brdo. It was from the opposite direction. So basically shells were landing in Srebrenica coming from four different sides. Weapons of different sizes basically because their sound was different --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones, you either control her yourself or I have to control her.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: She is running. I mean, she did not stick to the direction that you were trying to lead her to. Let's take them one by one, please --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. We've had the answer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And let's start with the first one Pribicevac or whatever --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Pribicevac. To summarise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: To summarise, you could see it with your own eyes. Is that correct? You could see the shelling coming from there with your own eyes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move to the next one. And you are in charge of her. And she could perhaps indicate on the map -- I haven't already circled it myself, but she could indicate on the map Pribicevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Hotic, if you wouldn't mind looking to your right there's a map there on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's the map on the ELMO that you have to look at.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, if you could first of all, and it's only if you can see it, but if you could see Srebrenica first of all and could point to that.

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Could you point to Pribicevac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Wait a minute, let's point to Srebrenica first.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is where Srebrenica is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So for the record the witness indicates with her finger Srebrenica on map D715.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's where the Stari Grad is. And that's where Pribicevac is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 13 minutes below Srebrenica she indicates Stari Grad, and at 25 minutes further to the east she indicated Pribicevac --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stari Grad is somewhere around here.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, let's deal with Sase. Can you locate Sase on the map, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I don't mind if Mr. Jones leads.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't read it really but it's somewhere here.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your finger is right there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Your finger is almost on Sase.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yeah, that's where it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record, the witness indicates Sase on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, how do you know, if you know, that artillery was firing specifically from Sase into Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Because the shells were landing from -- coming from that direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And how do you know that?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: On the basis of my sense of orientation I know where that is and we could see the shells were coming from that direction. Obviously since Serbs were holding those positions, that was quite clear, and it was quite clear that they were shelling us from Sase or from other surrounding villages or locations where they could place their weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you -- did you ever go to Sase yourself in 1992?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: After the -- it was freed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Just to follow His Honour's suggestion that we control question and answer. If I ask a question, you can give a simple answer and then I may follow up with further questions. So really my question is simply this: In 1992 did you go to Sase?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did you -- when you were there, did you or did you not see any evidence that shells had been fired from there?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were different sized cartridges or shells. There were heaps of cartridges. And I couldn't help wondering how we survived since all that had landed upon us.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And when did you go to Sase, roughly?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: At some point in autumn, I can't give you the exact date, when Sase was liberated, when the Serbs withdrew. And there was defence activity and Sase was freed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, I may not go into all the other locations you mentioned, Koprivno Brdo, Rogac and Tara. Can I just ask you this: Was this something which was discussed among the people in Srebrenica, including fighters, where artillery was firing from?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And was that not a source of information to as to where these missiles were coming from?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. But it doesn't really matter because I could reach that conclusion myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And then in terms of different types of missiles and artillery, tanks versus Howitzers or multiple rocket launchers, were you or were you not able during the course of 1992 and 1993 to distinguish the different sounds of what you heard?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the basis of the sound and on the basis of the place where the shells landed. Some shells left big craters. And their tail end or sometimes the mortar could fire 36 shells in one go, and they left a mark of a huge tail. There was the tail of the shell that would remain stuck in the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Would you if you heard the sound of a missile flying over, would you be able to say, That's a tank, or that's a Howitzer, or that's a heavy-calibre weapon or a small calibre?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. They had different sounds. Some had a terrible whistling, tearing, whistling sound. And of course the explosion would reverberate much more than a small mortar shell. And also some Howitzers, as they called them. If a house was hit, it would create holes in the walls. It didn't just go off as an explosion, whereas mortar shells exploded as soon as they touched a surface. So we could make a distinction between different types of weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. Are you familiar with Zoljas?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you ever come across their use during the war?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: I came to the place where Zoljas landed. They can cause a great deal of damage. For example, in my building a window was broken on the basis of that, and then they make holes in the buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you've described how when you returned to Srebrenica in May 1992 it was empty, more or less. Did it remain like that?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: For a long time until the UN came and then the Swedes did some repair work. They repaired some roofs and mended some of the holes and the rest stayed the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: There might have been a misunderstanding. What I'm referring to is empty of people. You mentioned how it was -- there were very few people in Srebrenica when you came in May 1992. Did Srebrenica remain sparse of people or did people arrive?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Yes -- oh, no. Already in May people started coming from Bratunac, mostly people from Bratunac who had been chased away from Bratunac. And they told us that they were betrayed there, that they had reached an agreement and they promised that they would remain loyal to the Serbs. And they even got fuel for agriculture and machinery. And then two days later Serbs started arresting people and other people ran through the woods and came to Srebrenica. And people were coming in on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'm not objecting, again, if Your Honours please, but I just want to follow the evidence carefully. My understanding is that the witness went into the forests on the 8th of May --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's when Goran Zekic was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And was there for a period of 11 days, I think she said in her evidence, eight plus 11, whatever we come to, I understand that she's now talking about these events at some point eight plus 11 --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We can clarify that --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I would be grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Di Fazio, and thank you Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you know approximately when Goran Zekic was killed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. She said already, she mentioned the precise date, she said 8th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. Let me put it this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: How long after the death of Goran Zekic did you return to Sebesic?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: After Goran Zekic's death we stayed only one more day in the forest. Perhaps there was a translation error. We were in the forest before and then we stayed one more night and then we went home.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. So that would mean you were in Srebrenica around the 9th or 10th perhaps of May. Is it right that you were in the woods for 11 days before that?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And then you've told us that refugees arrived from Bratunac in May. Is that something you yourself saw?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Because they started settling into my building. There were 16 Serb apartments in my building that were deserted by Serb families when they left so they were standing empty and people were moving into those apartments from the villages around Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. Well, let's deal first of all with Bratunac, the town, because you were referring there to an instance I -- instant where the Muslims were -- I think you said that they were tricked, that they were given petrol -- I'll need to check the transcript. But could you just tell us in summary what actually was the fate of the Muslims from Bratunac town in that period May 1992, what actually happened to them?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: When Serbs started arresting people in Bratunac, the ones that could not escape were taken to the school of Vuk Karadzic and 1.700 people were abused there. And Drago Zekic, Goran's father, actually tortured people and he killed them with wooden sticks and firearms. And when he took care of 300 people he said it was enough as revenge for the death of his son in Srebrenica. And then a number of people were exchanged later, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. and my -- and Slobodan Amacic from Bratunac, who was related to my husband was killed there. Many people were tortured and the Hodza of Bratunac was tortured a great deal. He was made to drink beer and to say Serb prayers. And also a police officer --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Sorry to cut you off, but it's helpful if you give brief answers and then I'll follow up. Firstly, just a clarification. You said Goran's father, when he took care of 300 people, he said it was enough. What do you mean he took care of 300 people?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: What I meant was that he killed 300 people to avenge the death of his son, and then he felt that it was enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. And how do you -- what's your source of information for these tales of what happened in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: In the beginning, people talked about those events. But as to this number, 300 people, I found out later from a prisoner who was also tortured there and who was exchanged later at Visoko I believe he was exchanged, his name was Bego. And he told me he was an eye-witness when Saudin was killed and he saw the way in which he was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, dealing with villages in Bratunac municipality as opposed to the town itself, can you name some of the villages where Muslims came from?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. Zaluzje, Voljavica, Bjelovac, Sikiric, I don't know, maybe Brezovica. And there were a couple of hamlets there from the area along the river Drina. People were flocking to Srebrenica, not all in one go, but gradually.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And so you referred to Bjelovac. Is it right, then, that Bjelovac had Muslims there?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Mixed population lived in Bjelovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. So if someone were to say that there were no Muslims in Bjelovac before the war, that would be false then, would it?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Of course it would be false.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I wonder if now might be an appropriate moment for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You've got two minutes left, but of course it's up to you whether you would like to stop here or take another couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In fact, I can ask one or two more questions and then it's a more suitable place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Even if we go beyond 10.30 for a couple of minutes, that's not a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you receive any information or do you have any idea of roughly how many Muslims were killed in Bratunac municipality in May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number, but very many people -- I mean, not everything was on record. Quite a few women and children got killed as well. A lorry was noticed that was driven to Serbia and a cousin of mine said that children were being taken by lorries to Serbia. Children were picked up somewhere in the course of those activities, and the exact figure is actually not known but quite a few.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: When you say "quite a few" or "very many," are we talking about 10? 50? 100? 200? 1.000? What roughly are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Several thousand.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And when these people came to Srebrenica, these people from Bratunac municipality, did they tell stories of what had happened to them?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Of course they did. They told us how they were tricked, how they had reached agreement with them, that there wouldn't be a war, that they would stay loyal to Serbs whatever happened, and then they were tricked. And they did not get organised, defend themselves, so they ended up as victims of crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did these --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment because there's a mistake in the transcript. So it will be line 15 on this page 37, that they would stay loyal to Serbs not whatever happened, nothing would happen and they were tricked -- at least the interpretation that I received was not whatever happened but nothing would happen. This was the essence of the trickery, in other words.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's how I understood it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's how I understand it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Correct me if I'm wrong, the witness is receiving interpretation. If that is not what she said, please do correct me. Otherwise, we go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may, perhaps I'm not going to use exactly the same form of words that I used before, but the meaning is the same, they agreed together, how shall I put it, to cooperate not to go to war against one another. That's the essence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Judge Eser.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Just for a matter of clarification. You have been asked how many people have been killed, and you told us quite a few women and children got killed as well as and a lorry was noticed that was driven to Serbia, and a cousin of mine said that children were being taken by lorries to Serbia. And then you were asked whether you could give a figure, 10, 50 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A cousin of mine, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Several thousand. Now, do you mean, several thousand people killed or several thousand people taken some there and, if so --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise. When I mentioned that lorry, I don't know how many children you can fit into a lorry, but what I meant was that in Bratunac many people were killed or went missing in the thousands, but we don't have the exact figures. It is very difficult to put an exact figure to it. But a cousin of mine who fled to Serbia saw a lorry that was driving in the direction of Valjevo, and there was a whole lorry load of children. And she was wondering why the Serbs would be -- would be loading children on to a truck.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop. Please answer the question that was put to you. When you said "several thousands," were you referring to -- did you mean to say several thousands of people were killed or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course if they're not alive today. They're missing persons, but none of them had come back so far. So it means they must have been killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I did have one final question to clarify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead, finish it. And I'm sure that the interpreters will agree to go on for just a couple of minutes more and then we'll have the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In discussing the trickeries, as you've described it, of the Serbs towards the Muslims in Bratunac, you referred to the Muslims being given petrol. What precisely were you referring to there? What trickery, if any, was involved there?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: In the area of Bratunac there is a great deal of agricultural land and it had to be planted. And since people could not get their hands on any fuel for their tractors and agricultural machinery, the Serbs gave them that fuel, and they were promised that they could work their land freely and that nothing would happen to them, that nobody would come to any harm.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So they worked their land and then they were expelled or disappeared. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. We will have a 25-minute break starting from now, which means we will start again at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, just at the start of the break the interpreter, B/C/S interpreter, contacted me. Prior to that she already contacted Madam Vidovic with a view to that correction done, and I quote "whatever happened," that part of the sentence. And she confirmed to me that it really been said as such by the witness. So "whatever happened" was the right quotation in the transcript. Because of that awareness, she notified me as well as the Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I don't think much turns on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Just one matter, actually, firstly Ms. Hotic, my apologies if I sometimes seem to interrupt you or cut you off; it's simply because it's easiest for us to follow if we have a short question and a short answer, so I trust you'll understand the reasons. Now, before the break you referred to the agricultural land in Bratunac. Can you just tell us roughly where in Bratunac are you talking about. Is it towards the Drina or towards Konjevic Polje? What part of Bratunac municipality?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: It's in the general direction of the Drina River.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, I'm moving now from the spring of 1992 to the summer of 1992, and again it's not in dispute that there were terrible conditions, lack of food, shelling, et cetera, in this period. So I simply want to ask you this: Did you ever go out of Srebrenica in order to obtain food?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. After two months in Srebrenica all the food had run out. We ran out of everything. The people who came from Bratunac, especially from the Zaluzje and Voljavica villages, said that they had lots of grain in storage, that they had food in their houses, and that they managed to sneak out during the night to see whether the Serbs were going around the houses at night and whether it was possible to go and get this food. When they made sure that during the night the Serbs mostly moved along one street down the asphalt street, and that they are not actually going into the houses, they decided to go and collect the food so that other people, too, who were not from Bratunac, because all of us together had spent all of our joint supplies, we went to Voljavica at night to collect the food. I was alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you mention an asphalt road. Can you help us with what road precisely that is. Where does it go between, that asphalt road?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: It's the road from Bratunici to Skelani. It goes along the Drina River, and that's the only asphalt road, the main road.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And you said -- let me just get this accurately. The Serbs mostly moved along one street, down the asphalt street. When you say "the Serbs," what exactly are you referring to? Are you referring to Serb civilians, Serb military, paramilitaries, what precisely do you mean when you refer to the Serbs in that context?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: It's general knowledge that all the Serbs were mobilised into the army. I don't know if they were called part of the military or a paramilitary groups. It's not important to me. They were all soldiers. They had weapons, they fired, they walked around.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: When you say they moved although this road, the Bratunac-Skelani road, were they moving on foot or in vehicles?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: They moved in vehicles and they would fire into the air as they passed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And what period does this relate to?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: It was autumn because the corn was ripe. Again, I don't remember the dates. We had taken the corn and the food from the houses and the storage rooms, and then when we ran out of that then we would pick the corn from the fields and along the road until we had picked everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, I want to just digress on one issue. You told us that your son was in a fighting unit. I think you said that at one point he joined Hakija's unit. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, did he encourage you to go out on expeditions to find food?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: No. I did that on my own. I wouldn't listen to my son or my husband because they didn't want me to do that. They said it was dangerous, and I myself knew that it was dangerous. But I thought that it would be even worse to die of hunger.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And when we speak about men who were in fighting units, at this time, and by "this time" I mean the latter half of 1992, was it possible just by looking at how a man was dressed, whether he was in civilian clothes or in a bit of uniform, was it possible to tell whether or not he was actually in a fighting unit?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: If you're thinking of Bosniaks, Muslims, there was no difference actually because people just wore whatever they had.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did your son have any uniform or part of a uniform?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: No, he didn't have a uniform at all. He wore jeans, a jacket, trainers.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you've told us that it wasn't -- you said it wasn't safe to go on these expeditions. Why not?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: After two or three such expeditions, they noticed that we left traces behind. We left traces behind. They could see our footsteps when we picked the corn. Then the road near Vejzovac, I heard that they set mines there so that people who went that way would set off those mines. And there were casualties. They also had a stronghold at Tara where they would fire bursts of fire. They also fired tracer bullets to light the area. That area was also mined. Three women were injured there. And very often they would also place the mines in the cornfields and the places where we would pass. So there would often be deaths and injuries as a result of that, and there were also prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you've mentioned Vejzovac. How far is that from Bjelovac, if you know. You can tell how long it would take in kilometres or how long to walk?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: I couldn't really say. You go into Voljavica directly through Vezovici. It's not far from Voljavica, perhaps a couple of kilometres, but I really can't say exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Shall we --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, we can see that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It shows on the map quite clearly, and to cut it short I think that I will try to indicate to the witness if I have the assistance of the technicians. We move towards the river, please, the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Drina River. Yes. You have to go further up, further up, yes, and more or less focus on the centre of the page of the map as we see it now. To the left a little bit, please, yes. That's it. Now, Madam, you see at the right next to the river there is the village or the town of Bjelovac. If you look to the west more or less in the same latitude you see Neskovici and further west to the left, Vejzovac.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Vejzovac, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: These are the two villages that you referred to earlier on. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you happy with that, Mr. Jones?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: How many times did you go on expeditions to this area, the Voljavica, area to get food?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: I went seven times with just civilians, regular people, to the Voljavica area.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Can you just describe for us -- just give us the names of the places you would go through from Srebrenica to get to Voljavica?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
