utterances.text: Through the village of Likari. When you leave Srebrenica and then go up the hill, then the first would be the village of Likari. Sometimes we would take the road, the forest road, just below Tablja, and sometimes we would go through Vejzovac. Sometimes we had to go along the river in order to avoid the mined areas. This was after we had already been a number of times and after people tripped on mines.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the place called Andrici?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Was that in -- was that Serb controlled or Muslim controlled in late 1992?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Of course, they had a bunker at Andrici because there would be shooting from Andrici. They would fire into the air at night.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, how long roughly would it take you to get to Voljavica on foot --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm afraid Andrici isn't actually on that map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can't see it on this map. Anyway, we have it on other maps.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. I think with one of the witnesses I attempted to locate it. Perhaps I can, if I'm permitted to lead on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: May I just ask. The village of Likari and this is the village of Obadi which you took?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Obadi is close.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Likari you can see. It's to the right of the red -- to the road marked in red.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And is Obadi -- is Andrici near or far from Obadi? I'm not sure if you heard the question, Ms. Hotic. Is Andrici near to Obadi or is it far from there?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: I couldn't really say. I didn't really notice where the villages were. It's all close to Sase, it's that area, Andrici, Obadi, it's all the same area. But I -- before the war I didn't really know that area. I never used to go to those villages. I just simply went with the other people, and whatever they said I would do the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And Caus, the hill Caus which we see there, when you went on these expeditions, was Caus in Serb hands or Muslim hands?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: It was mostly in Serb hands. Before or sometimes it was in our hands, but at the time it was in -- the Serbs were in control.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. And if you tell us roughly how long would it take you to get on foot from Srebrenica to Voljavica?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: As you go in the direction of Voljavica, it's about three or four hours, maybe three hours because we would be walking through the woods. On the way back, in the morning, only would you reach the outskirts of Srebrenica. You would be walking slowly, carrying things. So a lot of time was needed, but I never actually measured the time in hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And was there any way to get to Voljavica, apart from on foot, and were people -- Muslims in Srebrenica able to drive by car to that area at this time?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, in peacetime, yes, it's possible. But in wartime, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Now, do you know a place called Fakovici?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I don't think there's any dispute that's -- would you agree that's on the road -- the Bratunac-Skelani road?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you ever go there in 1992?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Once.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And when you went there, were you there alone or were you there during the course of an action?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: It was an action. We were looking for food, people had run out of food, so that we simply had to go and follow our fighters, even though they were telling us not to go. They kept telling us to return, but we simply had to go. We had to go and get food. So I did go to Fakovici, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You say the fighters were telling you not to go. If they didn't want you to go, why didn't they stop you and the other civilians from going?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Well, if Your Honours please, that's really a matter for the fighters, isn't it? I mean, they can answer. Unless of course --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: She knows.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: -- it was expressed to her, was she ever informed of such matter. But the way the question is framed, I have no objection to the topic of course, but the way the question is framed does invite speculation and that's what I'm concerned about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, obviously if she speculates, we'll stop her. And especially now that you have made your remarks she knows that she shouldn't to speculate.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Maybe I can rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think you even need to, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Maybe I can put it this way --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Let me put it this way: Were the fighters able to stop you from going to Fakovici?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Well, you can imagine a mass of people, thousands of people, who are hungry and stopping every fighter asking, What are we going to do, die of hunger? What are they going to do, kill us all. They simply went their own way and we did what we knew, the best thing -- we did the best thing we could.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, also to fix the date when you went to Fakovici, again I think there's no dispute there was an action in Fakovici on the 5th of October, 1992. Could that have been the date when you were there?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Probably, yes. As I said, I don't remember the dates, but the plums were ripe, the corn was ready for harvest because the vegetables and fruit ripened later in that area. But, yeah, I think that was around the time when we went to Fakovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And what made you decide to go to Fakovici on that day?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: To go and bring back food, because of food.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Why specifically Fakovici? How did you know to go there?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Because our fighters had decided to carry out an operation there, and we knew that there was food there because all the Serb settlements had food. And there was no other way to get to a place like that, so we took that opportunity. It was simply the only way to get to the food.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I think we had -- might have the issue again of the witness saying "aksija" and it interpreted as "operation." We've had this issue in the past and we say it should be translated as "action" not as "operation."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I agree with you, and the interpreters please note that whenever the word, Serbo-Croat word "aksija" is used, we would all like to see it translated into "actions" rather than "operations" in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, just maybe a preliminary question. When you went on expeditions to get food, did you go alone or did you go with any particular people?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: With many people. I wouldn't know how to get there. I wouldn't know the way, had it not been for a lot of other people. There were a lot of women.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you go with any friends, people you actually knew, on these expeditions?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. One of my neighbours was there, her name was Ismeta. I would always go with her.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, do you know, and if you're able to help us with this, how word got out or at least how you found out there was going to be an action in Fakovici?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly how the word got out, but we knew about each action. It would spread very quickly amongst the people. Probably every family had a fighter amongst them. Somebody would find out and that's how it would spread. It was not made public, but it was something that was known. People found out about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Was there a name given to you and other civilians who went into actions to get food?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. What name?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Was there a collect --

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Whose name?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Was there a collective name given to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you object, Mr. Di Fazio, if we go direct on this -- yes, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Were you ever referred to as a Torbar, Muslims going into action as Torbari?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. They would call us Torbari or Hapci.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, for you Torbari -- let's deal with Fakovici specifically. When you went into Fakovici, were you trying to follow the fighters or were you trying to avoid them or were you simply ignoring each other? How did that work?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: The fighters didn't look that much different from us, even fighters who had a rifle and civilians who carried a rifle. Somebody would go to a village and find themselves a rifle even though they were a civilian and they would keep the rifle. But I didn't really notice any differences between the fighters and us, the Torbari, except for the women. I knew that they were definitely not fighters.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, could you describe for us in Fakovici where you went and what you did on that day?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Mostly over the hills, through the woods using village paths. I couldn't really describe the exact road we took. Close to Fakovici -- in front of me was the Drina. Some of the houses -- I could see the roofs of houses of part of Fakovici. But I couldn't enter into some of the houses because of the shooting.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's deal with the shooting then. What precisely -- what sort of shooting was it? And if you can tell us, where was it coming from?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: One way which led to Fakovici -- well, many people had already entered Fakovici and I probably tried a little bit later or maybe I wasn't brave enough to be amongst the first people to enter it. And on the left-hand side, in the direction of Drina and Bjelovac, there were -- there was a lot of shooting there, and therefore I could not go down that road. And my group, the people I was with, we just couldn't go through because there was constant shooting. And so the hill that we came from was being shelled. There were shells coming from Drina, I think. So that I didn't manage then to Fakovici as such, and there was a house at the outskirts, and I was picking grapes and plums, and I got myself some corn in a field near the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you mentioned that you think the shelling were coming from the Drina. Now, obviously that's the river between Bosnia and Serbia. Was the shelling, in your view, coming from the Bosnian side of the Drina or from the Serbian side?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: It couldn't have come from Fakovici because people had already entered the town. It could have been from across the river because we were being constantly shelled from Nemici [phoen] and I don't know what the place is. But there are eye-witnesses to that and there were shells and bullets coming from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So who was sending the shells then, the Muslims or the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: I can state with absolute certainty that Muslims had no mortars, so even if they had held any such positions they wouldn't have been able to shell anyone because they had no mortars. So only the Serbs could have done that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And you mentioned that you weren't able to enter Fakovici because of the shells. Could you see where the shells were actually landing?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: The shells were landing above my head in the hills, but before the sounds of bullets being fired at the same time I was prevented from going down the road that I was intending to take because I would have been fired at.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Can you just firstly tell us what time this was roughly in the day that you were in the -- that you were in the outskirts of Fakovici?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Before noon.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And is it right then that at that time there were shells which you saw or heard falling in the area?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. And that accompanied me the entire time that I needed to go back.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. Now, did you see houses in Fakovici?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Parts of houses, parts of roofs and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you see any houses in Fakovici at that time which were in flames?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: I did not see any flames. I could see some smoke, but when Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. there's shelling there's always smoke, so it was normal. We could see smoke.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Are you -- at that time were you familiar with what it looks like when a house is set on fire as opposed to when it's damaged by shelling?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In terms of what you saw in Fakovici, in your opinion what was -- which case was it? Was it a house which had been set on fire or which had been damaged by shelling?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Well, if Your Honours please, I object to the question. Firstly, the witness was asked whether -- if she's familiar with what it looks like when a house --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: She said she saw smoke and not fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. And she was asked if she's familiar with what it looks like when a house is set on fire as opposed to when it's damaged by shelling. And she --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: She's already said that she didn't see fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we are running too fast, Mr. Jones, actually. I think you need to take it stage by stage. There is a point so far we haven't arrived at the stage where she has gone down into the town itself. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, and my point obviously was she's -- there's a distinction which she's familiar with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But then you can approach that once you have asked her whether she actually went down to the town herself and what she saw and whether she could distinguish one from the other, if that's the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because she hasn't said it as yet. So let's take it -- I leave it to you, of course, but let's take it stage by stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Firstly, did you yourself get into the centre of Fakovici?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And why not?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Because of bullets that had prevented me from taking that road. At the spot where I could enter Fakovici, I was prevented from doing so because lots of bullets were being fired at that time. So I simply picked in -- some corn in a field which was next to a house that was at the outskirts of Fakovici and then I went back.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And do you know who was shooting?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. What do you mean? Who was doing the shelling? Is that your question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not the shelling now. The shelling you have told us already. It's the bullets.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The bullets being fired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- the bullets that you were --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You know, our fighters would not have fired in that direction, so it means it must have been the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And from -- from where were they -- were they shooting? Was this from houses, or from across the Drina, or from fields, if you were able to estimate?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: I couldn't see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, I put to you earlier a distinction between -- which you stated that you could distinguish between a house which had been set on fire and one which had been hit by shells. Let's deal with them one at a time. How would you describe the appearance of a house which has been hit by shells? And actually firstly before that, did you see houses damaged by shells before in 1992?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. And can you describe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In Fakovici. Let's make it clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, I first wanted it to just be clear that the witness had actually seen a house damaged by shells anywhere so that she was familiar with the sight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And then I want to ask her to describe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If you could, Ms. Hotic, what is the appearance of a house when it's been damaged by shells?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: A house damaged by shells has holes in it, holes in the walls, and sometimes the roof may cave in. It depends on the size of the shell, and I saw both. I could have seen that in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And would there be any smoke or dust associated with a house being shelled?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Of course. Every shell, depending on the size, but at any rate it always creates a lot of smoke. I was suffocating by smoke myself but I hadn't been hit by the shell but there was a lot of dust and smoke.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. I'll come to Fakovici specifically but I'm still on this distinction. Now, you told us how when you were in -- the words "outside Srebrenica" that the Serbs torched houses. Could you describe for us what is, if any, distinctive appearance of a house that has been set on fire?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Apart from a spiral of smoke there is red flames and a different kind of sound from the shooting. There is a great deal of noise, and you see red flames shooting up into the sky.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And when you say "great deal of noise," what noise is that?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: A kind of breaking noise. I can't explain it, but it's very noisy, but it's not the same sort of sound as firearms being fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Let's go back to Fakovici now. Firstly, did you see houses which were intact which had no damage to them?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: I saw the roofs of the buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And can you estimate how many houses you saw where the roofs, they had their roofs, and they appeared to be intact?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Several. I saw several houses. I could see several houses from where I was, perhaps three to four.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, did you see any houses which, according to the description you gave earlier of houses which had been shelled, did you see many houses of that description?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: I was not close enough to those houses in Fakovici in order to be able to see properly. I did see that in other places.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you in Fakovici see any signs of houses which had been set on fire?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: When did you leave Fakovici that day?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: In the afternoon hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: How many hours did you -- did you spend there would you estimate?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: I don't know. From the morning until the afternoon, perhaps four to five hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And when you left, was the action still ongoing? Was there still combat action ongoing or was it over at that stage?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Shooting could be heard but not a lot of it. It was just that the shells were still coming and they accompanied us all the way uphill as we were heading back in the direction of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So shells were still being fired in that area when you left for Srebrenica in the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And do you know if any Muslims were wounded or killed during the Fakovici action?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: I could see very many wounded and some dead bodies as well that were being carried. I mean, one body was being transported on horseback. And there were civilians and women having been wounded, women who entered the village of Fakovici. There were very many wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And were these people wounded by shells or shooting or a combination of the two?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Both.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, if someone -- if someone were to say, I'll put it to you directly, that the entire village of Fakovici was burnt to the ground the 5th of October, 1992, from what you were able to see on that day would that be a true or false statement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Why are you using true or false --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I could see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment before you answer. Because if she wasn't there until the very end of the action she can only answer as to whether that would be an accurate, not necessarily true or false, whether it's an accurate or inaccurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Although as far as the action is concerned, and perhaps I need to revisit it, I understood her answer to be that the action -- the actual fighting of Fakovici was more or less over when she left, but there was still shelling --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're free to explore that, of course, but it seems until this point at least since something was happening there --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. I'll --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would rather you use the terms "accurate" or "inaccurate" rather than "true" or "false." Because the connotation is there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Certainly. I'll revisit it with certainly two questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: When you left Fakovici, were there still Muslims in Fakovici fighting or gathering food, or were you all leaving at that point?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: I left, but people were still coming out and heading back. It took a while, I don't know how long exactly. As to buildings having been set on fire, I can't claim that. There are still people there. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So let me put it this way: When you left Fakovici on the afternoon of the 5th of October, 1992, would it be accurate or inaccurate to say that the entire village had been burnt down?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: I can't claim anything either way. But I suppose not because people were mostly concerned about getting food.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you see when you left houses in Fakovici which were intact?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: I said I did not enter Fakovici myself. On the basis of the roofs I could see, the houses had not been damaged because since there were roofs that I could see, those roofs had not been damaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Is -- did you manage to capture any food in Fakovici?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: I said that I went to a field and I picked some corn, and I did not even have time to properly clean it. I just took lots of it as it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did you hear whether any weapons or ammunition were captured from the Serbs during this action?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Afterwards I heard that some captures had taken place, and that was normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did anything happen in Srebrenica after the action in Fakovici?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was lots of shelling at all times from all sides at Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did that occur after actions regularly or was this a one-off?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. After each action.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, after this action in Fakovici, was there enough food for everyone in Srebrenica to survive on through the winter?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: No. It was just enough for a couple of days or maybe more, ten to 15 days depending on how much you managed to get.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'd like to ask if the witness could be shown D545, please. And this is a document from the -- which purports to be from the subregion War Presidency, dated 20th November, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And it's right, isn't it, Ms. Hotic, that I saw this document with you here in The Hague, so you've seen it once already?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, I'd just like to ask you to comment on this appeal, as it's titled, and to say whether it reflects the situation in Srebrenica in 1992 as you recall it or not.

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: If I may, I'd just like to read it through once again to jog my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: We can continue now -- yeah, you can ask the question now.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, can you describe for us -- well, firstly are these events reported from November 1992 familiar to you? Is this how it was?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And if you could just help us with "generally the situation in November 1992," were there any instants or anything specific in November 1992 which you recall relating to the conditions of life?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: There was general hunger. All food had been eaten, and the reserves had been exhausted. And people started to eat anything that they could get their hands on, the husks of the corn or apple peels that used to have been left for the animals, and it was very difficult to digest that. And other -- sometimes elderly people would be taken for hospital, and I myself once ate that stuff and I was ill for a month. And the most difficult situation was for babies. You couldn't even have a spoonful of flour, and you just could not give that roughly ground stuff, basically bran, to little children. So the hunger was terrifying. So we didn't know what to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: May I stop you there, Ms. Hotic, for a moment because I want to follow up on a response that you gave there. You referred to people eating husks of corn or apple peels and that elderly people would be taken to hospital. Did anyone actually ever die from eating indigestible materials, or was it just a case of being taken to hospital and then recovering?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: I know that one man died in hospital. His digestive system just couldn't take it and the doctors could not help him. Even, to be honest, the doctors had nothing -- I mean, it was too late to help this man. I know of cases of death due to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did you know -- and again in this time, November/December 1992, of people actually dying from hunger?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Of course. One woman who had two children, she lived in a flat and she didn't go out for a few days, and basically after some time people went in and all three of them had died of hunger. Everybody had become Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. emaciated. It was a disaster. You could not tell the difference between young and old men, so to say. Everybody looked old. It was an extremely difficult time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Maybe an obvious point, but just to follow up on that. If at this time, November/December 1992, you saw someone who looked emaciated, tired, exhausted even, was that something out of the usual?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: No, everybody looked like that. Nobody looked normal. Both of my men, I mean my husband and my son, were just skin and bones. And my husband showed me how he just -- he rolled up his T-shirt and he showed me his stomach, and there was -- everything was empty. I could count his ribs. And I said, Oh, please, don't let me look at it, it's horrible. They all looked horrible.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'd also like to pass up another exhibit now -- it's not an actually an exhibit yet. It's a document of the command of the Birac Brigade in Milici. I have copies for everyone. There is an ERN which is 04337088.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And I'd like to ask you to look at this document because it's dated firstly -- or it refers to events on the 9th of November, 1992. It says: "On November 9, 1992, two Ustashas were killed in the area of Gunjak." Pausing there, when Serbs in that period used the word "Ustasha," do you know what they were referring to?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: They called Muslims Ustashas. Sometimes they called us balijas and sometimes Ustashas. Those were their names for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And this refers to an ambush being organised to stop groups of Ustasha, as they were called. From getting food. Let me just ask you this: In November 1992, were you aware of that going on in the Srebrenica area, people going for food and being ambushed?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Of course. Many people went looking for food in different places. I myself went on such expeditions 19 times altogether, sometimes following actions, following our fighters, and sometimes not on my own but in groups with out women. We were sneaking through the Serb-controlled territory in order to find food. And many women and many persons had actually been taken prisoner and they never came back. For example, in Bratunac whoever was arrested was never ever returned alive by Deronjic. And we don't even know about what happened to some people. They just went missing. Quite a few of those women were probably taken prisoner or killed but they never came back alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Could I ask for an exhibit number firstly for this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. This document is being tendered and received and marked as Defence Exhibit D716.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And just for clarification, you referred to Deronjic. Who are you referring to there? What name and what position, if any?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Miroslav Deronjic was in Bratunac from the very start of the setting up of the SDS party. He was in the Crisis Staff, and he was in Bratunac throughout that period. He had an important position in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you've mentioned Bjelovac already in your testimony. Did you ever go to Bjelovac during an action?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And are you able to locate that roughly in time either by the month or when it occurred in relation to the Fakovici action?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: I can't tell exactly what the period was between Fakovici and that, but this was late in the autumn. It was already winter. It was freezing. I think it must have been in December if I'm not mistaken, but I told you that I could not recall the exact date. When there was an action at Bjelovac, I wasn't there on that date, but I was at Loznicka Rijeka, which is in the direction of Bjelovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So firstly, you were in Bjelovac when there was -- well, not in Bjelovac specifically the town, but you were in that area when there was an action going on. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And you've mentioned a couple of days, so I would like to deal with it day by day. Firstly, again, did your son know that you were going to go to Bjelovac?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did, but he couldn't stop me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: But he was -- I take it he was opposed to you going?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: He was always opposed to me going. I told him, You do your job and I will do mine; don't interfere.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And you told me on the first day you went to Loznicka Rijeka, and we might just locate that on the map. Again, Ms. Hotic, I'm not sure if you'll be able to locate it on the map; it's not essential that you find it. But for our benefits, it's -- if we Sikiric and Loznica, in between we see written in blue ink Loznica R. So I'll just ask you: The Loznicka Rijeka you refer to, is that -- is that near Sikiric?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's near Sikiric, somewhere around there. It's Bjelovac. You can -- I know all of these places along the road. They are mostly linked.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, if could you just speak into that microphone.

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: I entered through the Pirici Brdo, which I see here, and I know I went down into Rijeka through Pirici Brdo. I passed through Brezovica; that's in a valley. There's a hill in front of it. You climb up the Pirici Brdo. It was very dangerous because there was strong shelling there. When there was fighting on in Bjelovac, it was terrible. I had never heard more shooting than I did in that very place.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll come to that. But so we see Sikiric next to Loznicka Rijeka. Roughly how far away would you say Sikiric is? Is it actually a separate location or is it a continuation of Loznicka Rijeka?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Perhaps a couple of houses and then another village. Those villages usually didn't have many houses. Then you would have fields and so on. I couldn't really say how far it was in kilometres, but everything was close by.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And again, did you go alone to Bjelovac or did you go with other people? And if so, could you estimate how many people?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: There were a lot of people. My friend Ismeta was with me, like she was always, she was my comrade in war. I entered a house near the Drina River, near the road in Loznicka Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm come to that in a moment. The people who went to Bjelovac or with whom you went to the Bjelovac area, were these civilians or fighters or a mixture of the two?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: That time I went with the civilians. At that time only, the Torbari or Hapci went. The fighters were already before in the fighting in the Bjelovac area.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And was the presence of these civilians, was that something which was organised by the authorities or by anyone or was it just people like yourself going along to the action?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: If I can respond with a question of my own. Which authorities? Which authorities do you mean? We didn't have an authority or authorities, legal authority in that period. It was just people. People organised themselves as they saw fit.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you've described earlier how at one point you were in Sase and you saw, I think, spent cartridges or something of that nature. Was that on this occasion or was it on some other occasion?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: On this occasion, too, but also before I saw that. Because the first time Sase was freed I was in Sase also. Perhaps I didn't say it before, but I did witness that for myself on two occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you pass through Sase on your way to Loznicka Rijeka on day one of this action?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was in Sase. I don't know which road we took to go over the hills. I really cannot remember which places we went through, but I know we came to Brezovica and then over the Pirici Brdo hill, and that's how I got to Loznicka Rijeka, through -- by going down that hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In Sase did you see any burned houses or property destroyed by fire?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: I saw damaged houses, you know, if they're hit by a shell and a wall is knocked down. But I wasn't really looking at the houses. I just walked through very quickly because there was nothing of food in Sase, so I was rushing to get to the next place.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you described how on day one you went from Pirici Brdo down to Loznicka Rijeka and you also referred to there being a lot of shooting. Can you -- can you describe that for us, as you arrived in Loznicka Rijeka, what sort of shooting, where it was coming from. Just give us a brief synopsis.

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Just over that hill, just going over that hill, I registered four types of heavy artillery. The shells were falling over the hill and then falling further away. I really don't know what type of weapons or ammunition this was, but I know that it was very difficult to go over this hill. The shells were coming from across the Drina River.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And what was the sort of frequency or intensity of the shelling?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: We waited for a kind of lull so that we could run over the hill, but this never happened. And then as we were going there and on our way back we didn't manage to get over the hill without the shelling. It wasn't a big hill, but the shelling was constant.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, what actually did you do when you got to Loznicka Rijeka?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: I went into a house and I found some other women there who were already looking for the food in the houses. There was a room. It was like a pantry or something, and there was different kind of food in there, sour peppers, bacon, I found rice, I found yeast for bread and that kind of thing. However, a shell hit the house and it broke through a wall, and the whole house shook and there was a lot of dust. So I just crouched down like the others, and we were all still for a little bit until it was over, but I didn't leave the house without taking as much food as I could carry. The same thing was done by my friend and the other women. The shell hit the house and then entered the house and exploded on the other side. That's what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, did you see any planes on that day?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. You could hear the planes going up river and downstream as well. You could constantly hear the airplanes and see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Were they doing in anything particular, apart from going up and down the stream?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: The shelling and the shooting was terrible, so I really couldn't tell whether the planes were bombing. There was different kind of shooting that day, and it was in the area of Bjlovci where the fighting was going on. I thought nobody was stay alive over there. We returned over Pirici Brdo, Ismeta and I and some other women. A shell fell very close to us. Some shrapnel flew by my nose. I thought I was wounded. I thought I could feel something dripping, but nothing happened. When we got to Brezovica we sat down to have a rest, but you could hear the shelling further down. I just want to say one more thing. When I was going up the Pirici Brdo hill, there was a small river there, and people were carrying food on horseback. A shell dropped and severed one of the horse's legs. When I turned around to see who was wounded, the people had already gathered around the horse, and they had cut up the carcass and took away the parts of the horse's body. And that's how I understood that they were actually going to eat the horse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. Now, still dealing with the first day and what you say on that day, did you see any houses on that day that showed signs of burning, having been set on fire, as opposed to having been damaged by shells or bombs, according to the distinction which you drew earlier?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: I state responsibly that no house was burning at that time. Perhaps if a house was hit by a shell, as it happened when I was in that house, but I could see that nothing was burning. I was amongst those houses. You could see smoke from the shelling further away or when a shell struck somewhere on a hill. And you could hear the loud noise of the shelling over there, you could see smoke, that was farther away. But the place where I was was clear. There was nothing there. There was some fighters also there. I could see them carrying a piece of meat, and they were slicing it up to eat it. I don't know if they had some kind of task assigned to them there or something, but I can state definitely that nothing was actually going on there where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And there where you were was the Loznicka Rijeka area, as you told us. Could you also see towards Sikiric?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I have a slightly more general question about the, sort of, houses which you were going into to get food from. And help us with this, if you will: Were there gas ovens in some or many of the houses which you -- which you saw or which are present along the Drina?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: I didn't notice that there were any gas stoves, but there were stoves that used wood or coal. However, many people had butane bottles or gas canisters, and they would use those for cooking. The cooker would be attached to this canister and then the gas would be turned on. That was the usual thing, but I don't know what you are asking me exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, thank you. Firstly these butane bottles, are they highly -- are they flammable, highly flammable, not at all flammable?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Of course the canister can be sparked off by a blow or something, and if a bullet or something like that hits it, then it can blow up like a bomb.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And again from your experience of going -- being in -- present in actions and from what you saw in houses where you went looking for food, would you have any explanation of how a house might go up in flames or be damaged, apart from it being deliberately set on fire?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: That's an invitation to a range of speculations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, I had already looked at you before you even reacted. Could you rephrase your question. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, I wonder if I might lead on a slightly different question. Of course it would be hard for my learned friend to say beforehand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On what part would you like to lead?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Specifically I'd like to ask whether this witness had experience of Serbs actually shelling their own warehouses, ammunition dumps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, do you have any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Go ahead, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Is that something which you are familiar, Ms. Hotic, Serbs shelling their own ammunition dumps?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: By accident? Deliberately?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Because again the same officer did it again. I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Sorry, I didn't realise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Make sure that it is switched off, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I apologise to both of you, both Mr. Di Fazio and Mr. Jones, because it irritates me, especially since it's the same person who did it before already.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, while that was going on, having looked at the question, I object to it. The question that Mr. Jones wants to ask is specifically: "I'd like to ask whether this witness has experience of Serbs actually shelling their own warehouses --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: -- ammunition dumps." If the question were to be rephrased such that did Serbs' bombs ever land on -- or shells on ammunition dumps, and as long as the witness can tell us how she knew there were ammunition dumps there, then I suppose the witness could describe that phenomenon. But I doubt that she'd be in a position to tell you whether or not the Serbs were deliberately targeting those -- any ammunition dumps that may or may not have existed. So I suggest that way out of the impasse --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I think that would be a good way out of this impasse, if it is an impasse at all. Do you have any objection of proceeding along the lines indicated by Mr. Di Fazio, Mr. Jones? I don't think that you should.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I think that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So, Ms. Hotic, if I can put the question again and I'll ask precisely as my learned friend put it. Are you firstly aware or familiar with Serb bombs ever landing on ammunition dumps or depots, either from your own experience or other sources of information?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Usually in the places where the Serbs were, they had significant quantities of ammunition and they knew about these depots. And when they were forced to leave the places, when we're talking about actions and so on, then they would fire at those depots to prevent them from being captured by Muslim forces. They could have done that from planes or any kind of weapon that had the proper range. That's what they would do. Sometimes I would hear the fighters say that it was very dangerous to torch a Serb house because it was possible that any one of them would have some weapons or something inside which could blow up and endanger people who were walking around looking for food. It was always the case that there were always people walking around looking for food. And the Serbs would then, in these cases when they couldn't take their weapons and ammunition out, fire at these weapons to prevent them from falling into Muslim hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mrs. Hotic, do you need a rest? Do you need a break?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. I apologise. I just have a chronic cough and sometimes I start coughing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's why I am asking you because the system here is that if at any time the witness would like to stop for a few minutes, you just have to say so and we will stop for as long as you wish. So it's no inconvenience to us and no problem to us at all.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'm not tired.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Hotic. Now, what was the source of your information or intelligence that the Serbs would do this, this thing of basically targeting their own depots or ammunition dumps when they had to withdraw? How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: From other people's experience. I was constantly in touch with other people, constantly talking to others, I was constantly on the move, and simply everybody knew everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You also said you overheard a fighter saying that it was dangerous to set fire to a house because of the weaponry and ammunition which might detonate. Was he saying this as an observation or as an admonition not to burn?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course it was an observation. It was something that was generally known amongst the fighters.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you -- let me put it this way: Did you ever hear a conversation in which fighters spoke out against burning -- burning houses or a specific fighter?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: I heard about Hakija Meholjic, that he would issue orders to his fighters not to burn houses. He said, Don't burn the houses. We will need the houses. Where are we going to put all of these people? They will come. They will have a house, they will have a field, they could live there and work the land. This is something that I actually heard from him personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, just dealing with the first day that you were in Loznicka Rijeka, did you -- did you stay in Loznicka Rijeka or did you go back to Srebrenica or did you go somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I returned to Srebrenica. Afterwards, I went to the Bjelovica area.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: The next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: On that day were there also civilians with you?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Of course. There was always a large number of civilians. I would be going with them. I wouldn't go anywhere by myself. I would be going with this large number of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. And on the second day did you actually go to Bjelovac?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was in the area of Bjelovac, but fighting was going on around Kunjerac. There was still shooting. It wasn't as much as the first day. I was in the cornfields picking the corn with Ismeta, with whom I always went. At that point a plane passed overhead that was firing rockets and dropped bombs in the area. I told Ismeta to lie down on the ground, but she said, Well, I hope something hits me so that all of this is over. Finally I've had enough of it. I'm sick of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you see houses in Bjelovac that day?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: I did see some houses, white houses were just there. I didn't go into any houses in Bjelovac because I knew that there was no food in the houses, and if there had been food that was probably collected on the first day already.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did -- among the houses you saw, did any of them have signs of burning?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: I didn't notice anything like that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you find any food in the Bjelovac area that day?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: I found corn. When I brought it home, it was only 11 kilos. But I decided to spend the night in a house in Voljavica with Ismeta, it was a house near the road, and we did spend the night there. Under the stairs in that house, there was a small area and that's where we found a sack of salt used to put that on the roads when it snows. And we decided to take that salt home and then use it for washing by soaking the salt in water. So we were very happy with that salt. We came home, we turned the oven on, and we baked a pumpkin that we had brought back. We didn't find too much food, but we went to the attic of that house and we found some beans. And then when we wanted to divide up the salt, we -- some man came by and he took this salt from us. So in the end, we didn't get the salt; it was taken away.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That was in Voljavica, was it, on the second day of this action -- or the evening?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. But this is all connected, that evening, and then the next day I went home. In the morning when we were getting ready to go home, at the crossroads of Bjelovica, Zaluzje, towards Sase, there was a group of women who had found some food. And I don't know, I guess they were discussing to go further. And in the meantime a shell dropped.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, yes. I'm sorry to cut you off but I'm conscious of the time and was going to move to another topic. Were there many -- do you know what sort of casualties were suffered on the Muslim side in the Bjelovac action?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: I think a lot of civilians were hurt. The highest number -- a lot of women were hurt, also a lot of the livestock. It was one of the most serious battles I think that had happened there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Is it right that you -- in Srebrenica you lived near to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, Marsala Tita street, number 86. That number still stands there today.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you yourself ever help in the hospital or visit there?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I took my sheets there, scissors. Whatever could help, I took there. There was so many wounded. They didn't have anything you could help them with because when the Serbs left Srebrenica they took away all the equipment, we didn't have any medicines left, so that we had general practitioners, doctors who had to do everything. They had perform surgeries, dress wounds, they had to do everything. When you go inside, you could smell blood, the flesh, people were wailing, screaming. Limbs were amputated without anaesthesia. They would give them some brandy to lessen the pain a little bit. A few times I was there. When I would start crying they would take me out and they would tell me, Don't come back anymore. You're more of a disturbance than you are of help. And I just felt that it was terrible what was actually happening there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you come across Dr. Nedret Mukanovic in hospital?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I knew him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Was he doing anything? Was he performing surgery?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. He performed surgery, but everybody did the impossible, what they knew and what they didn't know. Ivan Ilijaz, who was not a surgeon, did that, and Dr. Avdo and whoever found themselves there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And Ivan Ilijaz, if you can give us his surname, please, just for the record, and Avdo?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Ilijaz Pilav.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And Avdo?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: I can't remember, but I did know him well before the war. I can't remember his family name. His wife is called Zilha.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm actually about to move to another topic, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll have a break now and we'll resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One very quick matter. In the meantime, you will continue with your examination-in-chief and your colleagues will deal with it; same with Prosecution. Ibisevic's book, this morning we got the English version and it is P564E. I found out now that the Defence has already used various parts from this book, and the relative exhibit is D690. I want to avoid confusion in particular as we go along. So please tell me -- tell us tomorrow whether you want this translation as it should to remain as P564E and what's going to happen later on with -- when you are going to make use of this document, whether you are going to refer to D690 or whether you are going to refer to P564E. I mean, it's something that you need to do. The other thing is my attention has been drawn as to the possibility that there may have already been a C2. You sure there isn't?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: No, there is no C2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Please check again. I'm told that there may have been a map.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That was C1, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: C1, all right. Okay. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Hotic, after the action in Bjelovac which you've been describing, did the situation in Srebrenica with regard to food, did it improve, did it get worse, did it stay the same?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: After Bjelovac and after we managed to get some food, it all lasted for a very short time in Srebrenica. Things continued to be difficult. First of all, not everybody could get food, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, did you -- or firstly, are you familiar with Kravica?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was at Kravica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: When were you in Kravica?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: I know that it was on Serb Christmas day. It was the beginning of 1993. There was a lot of snow, and it was the worst possible time in terms of hunger for Srebrenica. Also, everything had been covered by snow. There was nothing left and people were literally starving to death.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: When you say "everything was covered in snow," did that have a bearing on the food situation?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Of course. And because what was left behind in the fields that we could get our hands on had disappeared because frost and snow had destroyed it all. You could get nothing at all. We, for example, used to go looking for hazelnuts and there were no hazelnuts left, and there was no wood left to burn. There was literally nothing left.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, when did you hear that there would be an action in Kravica?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether on the day before or on the day that the action took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And from whom did you hear that there would be an action?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: From the people. That kind of news travels fast, in a low voice, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. but everybody gets told.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, at that time did the place, Kravica, mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. The place of Kravica meant that it was a big strong Serb military stronghold. It was a threatening place. You did not interfere with that. It was like a nest of hornets, but that was the only way to get food because it was -- you either live or die.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do I take it from that the people in Srebrenica were afraid, in some sense, of Kravica?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And at this time in January 1993, or rather what you've described as it a big strong -- Serb military stronghold, a nest of hornets, does that apply to that period, January 1993, or before or what precisely?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, it was generally well-known about Kravica. Even before the start of the war, we knew that the Chetniks that were left over from the Second World War had stayed there. So that was their area where they had their roots. So people tried to not go too near Kravica and -- if you didn't want to meet with these people. So you just avoided the place.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And again, as far as you knew or were aware, were the fighters in Srebrenica keen that you and other civilians should go to Kravica or were they opposed or were they indifferent? What was the position?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: They were opposed, the fighters were opposed. First of all, they were even opposed to the idea of launching an action against Kravica. But the people insisted -- they kept begging them to do something. You said, You have to do something, you must do something, otherwise we'll all starve to death. What is this fate that has befallen us? And nobody actually believed in a really good outcome, but it was a must. We were forced to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm going to be referring to D714 for the map because the previous map doesn't actually have Kravica on it. So again, perhaps if the witness could have that by her on the ELMO. If we could try and have the section which would show Srebrenica and also Kravica. So we have Srebrenica, and if we could just lower it -- lower the paper a little bit -- or sorry, the other way. And a little to the -- well, so the left of the page is visible. Yes. Could we have the left of the page and then lowered slightly. When I say "lowered," a bit higher there, other direction. A bit more, bit more. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, do you see Kravica on that map, Ms. Hotic?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Kravica is somewhere here.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... there. You were pointing --

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: I can see Repovac here, Hranica -- Kravica is in this area but I can't see it written down here. It is somewhere behind Rebrovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. If you -- I assume there wouldn't be any objection if I direct you --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Kajici, it's in this part because this is from Bratunac --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Wait a minute. You see the road going from Bratunac towards Konjevic Polje?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Follow that road along a little bit you'll see Magasici - keep going - you were at Hransaca [phoen]. If you keep your finger running along the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I have no objection to Mr. Jones approaching the witness and pointing her --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I told him go ahead already.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. I'm just trying to get her there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And a bit further along to your left, you'll see Kajici and then Kravica. Just keep following along, Ms. Hotic, with your finger and you'll see Kravica on your left. A bit further.

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Kajici. Yes, that -- there it is. I do apologise. I don't quite understand the map, but I know the general direction. But now I've found Kravica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record, the witness points at Kravica with her finger.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, could you just mention the names. You don't have to trace it on the map; in fact, you can leave the map, Ms. Hotic. We can follow it ourselves. Ms. Hotic?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If you could just mention where you went, the villages or hamlets that you went through to get to Kravica on the Orthodox Christmas.

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: When I went to Kravica I went in the direction of Potocari from Srebrenica, and in Potocari -- in the direction of upper Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you --

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: And the people who were with me said that we would go across Susnjari, Jaglici, and then we would go down, down the asphalt road to Kravica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Is that the route you took: Potocari, Susnjari, Jaglici, Kajici, Kravica?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: I think so, yes. Everybody went down that road. We actually created a path in the snow.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Is there any reason you didn't continue along past Potocari towards Bratunac? Did anyone give you any directions or any suggestions as to where you should go?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Of course there were Serbs at Bratunac. As of Zuti Most, we could not go down, and you couldn't take the road down to Potocari through Potocari because we would have shelled from the hill Zvijezda Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Just for the record, I think we should have that hill spelled, Zvijesda. Could you spell it for us letter by letter?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Z-v-i-j-e-z-d-a.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In fact, the stenographer got it right the first time, so ... Thank you. Now, can you estimate just roughly how many people were with you when you went to Kravica, whether it was 10, 100, 1.000?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: I think everybody who could walk actually walked to Kravica. And there were about 60.000 people in the Srebrenica at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So we're talking about thousands of people going to Kravica?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: What time roughly of the day did you arrive in Kravica? We don't need an exact hour, but morning, afternoon, late afternoon, evening?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Early evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And was the military action still going on at that time, when you arrived in Kravica?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It was over?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: When you went on this route which you've described through Jaglici, Susnjari, Kajici, Kravica, did you see any houses burning?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Yes -- no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I believe the witness was saying yes in the description of the route and then answering no to my question. I'll put the question again. Did you see any houses burning on that route?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: I did not see any houses burning.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you go into the centre of Kravica?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: From the main asphalt road I went into a warehouse, and somebody in that mass of people had told me that there was a lot of food there, but everything had been taken already because from the morning people had set off to Kravica and I had come across people coming back carrying food. Some people were coming back as we were going to Kravica. Only in the area of Jaglici when I was going down, we were shelled. There were shells landing in the direction of Jaglici and we could not hear any other sounds of battle, shooting.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Are you familiar with a place called Jezestica?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's close by as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Close --

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: But I don't actually know the village itself. I know where it is approximately, but I've never been to the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You were describing Jaglici. Do you mean it was close by Jaglici?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: It's not far.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: How long did you spend in the Kravica area that day?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: I don't know if I spent two hours there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you spend the whole time near the road, the Bratunac-Konjevic Polje road, or did you go away from the road into the hills a little?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Perhaps a couple of houses in the direction of the hills, because the first houses were empty, everything had been taken. So I hurried, I actually ran to a house, and in a pantry or some sort of kitchen I found a great deal of food there, corn and wheat, and I found two-kilo packets of white flour and I took as much as I could.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: No objection. It's just that perhaps -- in fact, I may be will to assist Mr. Jones and also myself. He asked: Did you go into the centre of Kravica? And the witness gave a long answer. She talked about going into a warehouse. She didn't actually say whether she had gone into the centre --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I agree with you entirely, Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. There might be a definitional problem of what the centre is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Are you familiar with where the church is in Kravica?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: The church is at the top. I did not go as far as the church. The only church I know is somewhere on the top. I don't remember. But when I was in Kravica I did not actually know where the church was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Would you be familiar with the primary school or any of the buildings which would be in the town centre in Kravica?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: I really am not able to tell you what the centre of Kravica is. It is not a big village. It might have between 30 and 40 houses, I don't know. Before that I had only travelled down the road through Kravica, but I never paid any attention to where everything was. At that particular time, though, my main aim was simply to get the food.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Let me also just ask you this: The warehouse which you've described, was that either before you reached Kravica coming from Kajici, or was it after, on the way to Konjevic Polje, or was it in Kravica itself?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: You mean the warehouses -- warehouse for food? It was at Kravica in the direction facing Bratunac rather than Konjevic Polje. I think that's where it was. As far as I can remember now. I mean, this is ten years ago so -- and at the time I wasn't really thinking in those terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Just to summarise this, would you say that you were in Kravica that day?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was in Kravica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'd like the witness to be shown P400 briefly which comprises a number of photographs. I have a dozen or so. In fact, she can use my copy if it's quicker -- oh, no, we have it ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Ms. Hotic, I'm simply going to ask you to flick through these photographs and to tell us whether you -- on the 7th of January, 1993, whether you saw any houses which were in this state -- well, let's start with 01087891. When you were in Kravica, did you see any buildings which were in that sort of a state?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: I saw undamaged houses in Kravica. And people running through the houses looking for food and clothes and shoes because they had nothing to wear either, but I saw not a single house looking like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In fact, I think that disposes of it. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, leaving aside houses for the moment, on that day did you see any other -- did you see any objects which had been set on fire or which were on fire?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Hay was on fire only, but it provided light for us so we could see where we were going. That was the only thing that was burning. I think where I entered in the direction of Bratunac, not Konjevic Polje, the only thing that was actually on fire was hay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you about that in a moment. But firstly when you arrived in Kravica, was it light, was it dark, was it twilight? How much natural light was there?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: It was twilight. I could see -- it wasn't pitch dark. It was in the early evening hours, twilight.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Because I could see clearly the road that I was walking along and it was close to a creek. And I could see that the house that I went in was a new one, and this shed that I found the food in had also been new.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, going back to the haystack for a moment was that --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Well, if Your Honours please, the witness didn't said "haystack," she said "hay," and it's of some importance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, you are right. Yes, I would agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: My apologies. I might have jumped the gun.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Maybe you can ask her also because I'm still wondering in my mind exactly what we are talking about, because at one point in time she said Kravica is a small place with just about 40 or 50 houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The town itself, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If she could identify at least -- if she could, if she couldn't obviously it's not -- then we stop there, any landmark, any particular building that she could distinguish. Say, you mentioned a church, you mentioned --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: A parish hall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Parish or whatever. If she could identify. I also do realise that she said that she had passed from that area before but not really knew the place. So this -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, perhaps with the warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
