utterances.text: You mentioned a warehouse, Ms. Hotic, were you actually familiar with a warehouse beforehand as being in Kravica or was that the first time you laid eyes on it?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: No. When I entered Kravica somebody said that there was a warehouse there for food. I did not know about it. I did not have any prior knowledge of that warehouse. I just followed the crowds, but I entered the building. I can't really remember correctly where it was. I just realised that it was empty and I went on, and I hurried to find something that had not been taken away as yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Let me put it this way: How did you know that you were in Kravica and in Kajici on that day?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Because everybody was in Kravica and, first of all, there are no other houses in the vicinity of Kravica. You go to Kravica from Konjevic Polje and then you have a string of villages. But yeah, I know where Kravica is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: When you're referring to Kravica, are you referring to the commune or the village?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: The village, whether it was called anything else before I never asked. Whether it was a municipality or not, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. Now, going back to this hay, the hay you saw burning, can you describe that for us. Was this hay lying around on the ground or was it organised in a stack or was it in some other way stored or arranged?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: When I say "hay," what I mean is hay which has been put away for winter, so it is of course haystacks. And a haystack like that was burning and that's what I saw. It's not scattered on the ground. It was in a haystack, if that's what you call it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And this haystack, was that in a field or was it in a barn?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Well, the houses were there and then there would be an area around the houses, gardens, fields. The houses were not close together, maybe a couple were close together, but they were scattered with gardens and fields around the houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Dealing then with the haystack, did that generate some smoke, a lot of smoke, no smoke? What sort of smoke was generated by the burning of the haystack?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: I didn't really look to see if there was smoke, but you could see the flames, the red flames. That was what I could see, that there were a lot of flames.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And before this day, had you seen haystacks on fire before?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: I don't remember seeing that anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So what I wanted to ask you is if you -- only if you can help us with this, but does it make any difference in your experience to how much smoke is given off by a haystack, whether it's wet or dry?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Hay smokes a lot, but it was night so you could see the illumination better. I was very close so I could see the flames -- the hay in flames. As far as the smoke, it was mixed up in the air so it was very difficult for me to see exactly. But I do know I saw in other places when something is burning, when a pile of hay is burning that's a little damp, then there is a lot of smoke. If it's not very dry, it can smoke a lot. That's the difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. And on this day, was it --

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: That's what the kind of flame would depend on.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And on this day, was it -- was the ground dry or wet?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: The ground was covered by snow.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: And the hay could have been dry because once it starts burning, the top that's covered by snow -- but, I mean, I wouldn't really discuss it that much. I don't know how important that is. It was hay and it was burning and that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, I think you've told us, correct me if I'm wrong, that you did actually find some food. Did you -- did you manage to take food back to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: I took twice as much food that I could carry. I put 30 kilogrammes in my backpack, and I counted it because the flour was packed in two-kilogramme bags. It was fine flour. And I packed 30 kilogrammes in my backpack. And then I also put another 30 kilometres [as interpreted] in a plastic crate, and I found a kind of plastic rope or something and attached it to the crate, and I dragged that through the snow. So I took double the load that I could carry, hoping that I would manage somehow.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you see any other Torbari on that trip bringing food back in a similar fashion?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Of course people were carrying things and then some of them were coming back again to get food. A man was carrying two 50-kilogramme sacks. He would carry one 10 metres, put it down, and then return to get the other one. And that's how they did it. I asked him, How are you going to carry all of that back? He said, Well, it's worth my while to carry back one week's worth of food because there is nothing else. People were carrying stuff up the hill. I met one 12-year-old girl. Her name was Irena. She was living in my building with her mother and her nine-year-old sister. Irena was carrying some potatoes and sauerkraut on a lid. I said, Irena, couldn't you find any flour? She said, Well, we have some rice. She was only 12 years old. She said her mother was lying down, she couldn't get up because she was so hungry. Her mother's name was Nevzeta. And this child had gone on her own together with the other people to look for food. You can imagine what trouble drove her to do something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you go back to Kravica after that day, the Orthodox Christmas?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: No. When I came home I really couldn't move at all. It took a long time for me to recover. It was very difficult for me to carry and drag that load up the hill. At one point, one young man who was carrying a sack of his own pulled the rope that I had, so he helped me carry that up the hill. I was very thirsty. I ate a piece of roasted meat in Kravica. One of the women probably gave it to me. And it was a long time since I had had anything like that to eat. And I was very thirsty. So on top of all the other trouble, I had to eat snow on the way in order to quench my thirst. But when I got home I was very, very happy. I had come home with 60 kilogrammes of flour, but there was no way that I could go back again. Other people, some people, kept going back and forth for two or three days to bring out more food.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: There's an exhibit which I'd like to hand up now which we have copies of for everyone. It has the ERN 04363125. I should say it's from the Drina Corps archives. And the title is regular combat report. It's from the command of the Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And I'd ask you -- firstly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Jones, let's have a look at it. Okay, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Firstly, Ms. Hotic, would you agree that I showed you this document when you came here to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, there are some place names mentioned Polom, Ocenovici, Supotnik. Are you familiar with those places or some of them?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. Polom is downstream from Bratunac, down the Drina. When you go from Bratunac along the Drina, it's an old road. It's not used anymore because it goes through Konjevic Polje and it goes towards Drinjaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And Ocenovici, are you familiar with the name at least of Ocenovici?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: I don't remember the name Ocenovici. I hadn't heard of that before.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We'll find these places on D714. I simply want to ask you this: Reading this document are you familiar with this phenomenon from 1992 or 1993 of Serbs booby-trapping or mining houses in order to kill Muslims when they went for food?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: I know that Serbs would mine places where grain was held, and they would leave that at places where people would try to sneak up during the night in order to get some food. This would happen in places along the Drina River around Bjelovica [as interpreted] because I would come through Orlica before regardless of the combat actions. I would come with the people to the fields looking for food. So that people in their attempts to get to the food would trip mines and that's how people got hurt.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Just two questions. You said Bjelovica in the transcript --

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Bjelovac. I'm thinking of the area of Podrinje, that part from Bjelovac. I would go through that area with the people regardless of the combat actions. I went to look for food 19 times during the war. Sometimes it would be along with the action and sometimes it would be separate from that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And -- thank you. And as far as actually houses being mined, mines actually being planted in a house, as is referred to in this document, is that something you ever heard about or understood to have happened?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I heard about that. They would place mines along the road as well as place mines in the houses. They were like traps. The house would look attractive, look as if perhaps there was some food there, and many people were killed or injured in places like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It was a mousetrap [Realtime transcript read in error "house trap"]?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'd ask for an exhibit number, please, for this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, this will become Defence Exhibit D717.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I actually said "mousetrap" rather than "house trap".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I know that, but sometimes there are house traps as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: There's one more document which I think I'd like to deal with today depending --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. More or less, Mr. Di Fazio, having heard roughly almost all the evidence, how much time do you think you will require for cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: A good part of tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If not all of tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I think I'll only be another 20 minutes, half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Do you think you would be able to finish with the witness if Mr. Jones takes another 15 or 20 or 30 minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You mean 15 or 20 of tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I don't think that will be a problem, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then we can stop here rather than proceed any further because I wouldn't like to keep anyone else beyond the -- unless it is really necessary, and everyone has always been so cooperative. So I would rather we stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, that's perfectly fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam, I thank you so much for bearing with us. We will continue tomorrow morning at 9.00, and we hope to be able to finish with your testimony tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too. It is very important to me, Your Honours, to uncover the truth. I have been fighting for ten years now to uncover the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One more thing I have to tell you before we leave and that is that between today and tomorrow please do not communicate with anyone and do not let anyone communicate with you on the subject matter about which you are testifying. All right? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 25th day of August, 2005, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.44 p.m.,
